projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Albert Bitonio was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: This following interview is of the Veterans' History Project, Washington, DC, Library of Congress, and it's taking place on January the 5th, 2006, in San Pedro. And the interviewee or the veteran's son is Albert, A-L-B-E-R-T, Bitonio, B-I-T-O-N-I-O. And his dad, who is deceased and served in two wars, is Macario, M-A-C-A-R-I-O, Bitonio, B-I-T-O-N-I-O. And I am the interviewer. My name is Robin Williams. R-O-B-I-N, W-I-L-L-I-A-M-S. Good morning, Al.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Good morning.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: First, I wanted to ask you which wars your father was involved with.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: World War I and World War II.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: And did he enlist or was he drafted?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He enlisted.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. What did your dad do before he joined the service?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He was living with his parents at home.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Was he in school or --

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He was -- he had just finished school and he decided to join the Navy to become an American citizen.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And where were they living, the family?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: The family was living in the Philippine islands.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Why did your dad, as far as you know, join his branch of service?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He joined the Navy because that was his way of becoming an American citizen.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Thank you. As far as the attack on Pearl Harbor 1941, do you happen to know about what age your dad would be and what he might have been doing at that time, maybe in school? I know they heard it on the radio. There was no television in 1941.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He was 50 years old and he was at home, I believe. I can check his age for you if you'd like me to.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Okay. He was at home. He had been in the service. He was out of the service and he was just home at that particular moment in time.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. Al, where did your dad serve when he was in the service? You know, maybe you could even tell me where he was in boot camp and training, basic training, you know.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Well, I think when he joined the Navy he -- his basic training was -- probably took place on the ship. Because he was -- at that time all the Filipinos were in the kitchen because they had -- at that time when he joined the service that was the only thing they could do. World War II he landed with the 1st Marine Division in Guadalcanal. He was with the construction battalion.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Thank you very much. And where did he serve?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: World War I he served on various ships such as The Rochester, The Oklahoma. There's a few others. I can't remember what they are at the moment.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: They're being sent.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: But you'll get that information. World War II he landed with -- as I said, he landed with the 1st Marine Division in Guadalcanal and he was there for the duration.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Thank you. And his job assignment was?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He was a cook.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And your father saw a lot of combat probably in the service.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: In the service, especially World War II, being in Guadalcanal, he saw a lot of combat.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Could you discuss maybe what you think or have -- know that might have been his most memorable experience while he was in the service? Or there might have been more than one, maybe the more positive.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Probably his most memorable experience in World War I -- well, not really. After World War I, I guess, was becoming an American citizen. World War II, I think it was just getting a little bit of time off in Guadalcanal and going to another island for rest and relaxation.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And as far as casualties in his unit, on the ships, probably?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: The ships I'm not too familiar with. World War II 1st Marine Division, Guadalcanal, the Seabees, a lot of them were just wiped out. I mean, there was -- the casualty was -- casualties were high. And that's in any of the naval history.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Right. Do you think your dad was ever fearful during the time he served in the wars?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: I think anyone serving in a war is fearful when someone's shooting at you.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And the food and provisions where he was in different places?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Well, because he was -- he was with -- he was a cook in the commissary department, he -- the provisions came from various sources. Some -- he used to buy stores for the ships during World War I. World War II, I have to assume they were shipped in and distributed accordingly.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. Any pastimes, recreation during the time he was serving?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: The only thing that I'm aware of, that he went to New Caledonia and he bought my mother a bracelet made out of part of a Japanese airplane, a wing of a Japanese airplane. It's very small and I have it and I'll keep it forever.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Which is, by the way, sitting on the table near us right now and it's a beautiful silver bracelet. Beautiful. Okay. What about the mail, the mail that went out and was received?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: The mail that went out that my mother wrote at times might have been censored. The mail we received from him was censored because there was pieces of it cut out, so a lot of it didn't make sense because the words were cut out and there's big chunks of it gone. You don't know what's being said for sure.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Not connected.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Absolutely. Okay. And holidays. Do you think they were able to celebrate holidays, Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: I think they might have celebrated the holidays somehow in their own way. Look at various -- you read various things and you see various pictures of service people and you see they take a little piece of a tree and decorate it to the best of their ability with tinfoil or whatever. I think they celebrated. I know that he sent V-mails for holidays to my mother and to various people which I have copies of.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Um-hum. Thanks, Al. Okay. And as far as -- and you mentioned something before to me, but I'd like to get it on record here. What skills or lessons do you feel that your dad learned in the service?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Survival. How to survive, especially in World War II. I don't think in World War I -- there was -- we -- there was survival too, but being on various ships, you were going here and there and all over.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. Survival seems to be the main instinct a person has. Okay. Where was your dad when he left the service? Where was he stationed when he was about to leave?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And where was he when the war was over?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And in the days and weeks after the service he just --

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He just came home and he tried to kick back and relax and get back with the program, see what was going on in the United States.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And as far as friendships go when he was in the service, did he make friends?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: He had many friends, especially when he joined the Navy, because most of the Filipinos that joined the Navy with him, they became lifelong friends. When he passed away in 1981, there was many of them who were still alive that came to his funeral, and he was 89 at the time. So it's a enduring friendship.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Um-hum. Okay. And after the war his career was?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: After the war and after he had time to relax and take care of him he went to work at Fort MacArthur in the kitchen.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: That's a good place to work. And his wartime career obviously contributed to that, because he did that.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Oh, yes. He was a wonderful cook forever and ever and ever.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Um-hum. Taught his son how to cook too.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. How would you say -- if your dad was sitting here now, how would you say he would -- what would he say would be -- would contribute to his thinking about war and military service as it is now since his service?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Well, it's changed considerably. He was a Navy man from day one until the day he died, whether he was in the service or not. In this day and age, it's a lot different. He wouldn't probably be very happy with a lot of the things that are going on, and yet he would accept it, because he always accepted whatever the role was at the time.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Thank you. Was your dad a member of any veterans or other organizations related to his service and went to meetings and reunions and that?

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Yes. He was a member of the Veterans of Foreign Wars and he was a member of the Fleet Reserve Association and he did go to the meetings.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. Well, I think we've covered just about all the questions. It seems that your dad had a strong desire to serve his country.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: You know, and that was what kept him going there.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robin Williams
sp.p: Okay. And I want to thank Al Bitonio, Macario's son, today for sharing with us with the Veterans' History Project. And we'll sign off now.

sp.speaker: Albert Bitonio
sp.p: Okay.
